title: Beyond Buildings: ArchDaily's November Editorial Focus
text:
Beyond Buildings: ArchDaily's November Editorial Focus

"Design a cultural center on a desert coastline, in the style of Alvar Aalto, wood structure, golden hour, aerial drone shot, photorealistic, 4K." Within seconds, a line like this returns a convincing image. What is less visible is the shift it demands. For centuries, architectural imagination relied on the body: the hand that sketches, the fingers that shape a model, or, more recently, the click of a mouse in computational tools. Words came afterward, to explain what had already taken form. Today, the order is increasingly reversed. Before an image can exist, it must first be described: its references named, its materials listed, its mood specified.

title: A Walk on the Roof: Linnahall and Tallinn’s Shifting Shoreline
text:
A Walk on the Roof: Linnahall and Tallinn’s Shifting Shoreline

From the end of Mere Boulevard in Tallinn, Linnahall appears as a long, low mass of limestone and concrete laid between the Old Town and the bay, kept deliberately beneath the line of the medieval silhouette so that the spires remain visible from the water. Broad stairways climb its flanks to a roof paved as a public square, and from there a sequence of terrace steps down toward a small pier, a helicopter pad and the open Gulf of Finland. Under that surface sit an amphitheater for 4,200 people, a foyer of 6,000 square meters, an ice hall, cafés, a bowling alley and a recording studio.

title: Designing Furniture to Outlast the Fit-Out
text:
Designing Furniture to Outlast the Fit-Out

Furniture waste is not always the result of physical damage that renders a product unusable. Chairs, sofas, and tables are often discarded because they no longer fit an interior concept, are perceived as outdated, or are replaced during a renovation. In many cases, their structures remain functional, even when upholstery is worn, or the surrounding space has changed. The result is a cycle of replacement in which usable products become waste, while new resources are extracted and processed to manufacture their successors.

Pritzker Prize laureates Anne Lacaton and Jean-Philippe Vassal have been announced as the recipients of the 2027 Le Prix Charlotte Perriand. Organized annually by the Créateurs Design Awards (CDA), the prize recognizes practitioners whose contributions have advanced architecture and design through a peer-led voting process. For its eighth edition, the organization highlighted the work of the French architectural studio as a demonstration of "how the adaptation of existing structures can improve living conditions while preserving resources and architectural heritage." Previous recipients of the prize include Xu Tiantian; Kazuyo Sejima and Ryue Nishizawa; Frida Escobedo; and Jeanne Gang.

text:

House in Dahiya gives nothing to the street. On a quiet road in Dahiyat Abdullah Al Salem, one of central Kuwait City's most premium residential districts, a stepped mass of raw exposed concrete rises between two date palms. Its principal facades are closed, and the entrance sits back behind dark vertical fins. The brief asked for exactly this: a house closed and unreadable from the street, yet open, light and generous within, and able to withstand Kuwait's heat, dust and salt air with little upkeep. Behind the sealed mass lies a protected inner world with its own climate, color and calm.

title: In the Wake of the 2024 Floods in Southern Brazil: Restore the Past or Rethink the Future?
text:
In the Wake of the 2024 Floods in Southern Brazil: Restore the Past or Rethink the Future?

In May 2024, the floods that hit Rio Grande do Sul exposed a contradiction common to contemporary cities. Many were built alongside rivers and shaped by their presence, yet spent decades trying to control water without incorporating its dynamics into urban planning. Extreme weather events will intensify that vulnerability. More than two years later, reconstruction in the Brazilian state has progressed, infrastructure has been restored, and new protection strategies are taking shape. But are these cities rebuilding their relationship with water, or only restoring the systems that failed?

title: "Nothing Starts From Zero": In Conversation With Sarah Hejazin and Bisher Tabbaa of FADAA
text:
"Nothing Starts From Zero": In Conversation With Sarah Hejazin and Bisher Tabbaa of FADAA

Following a seven-year pause, Amman Design Week returned in 2026 under the theme "Accumulations," bringing together designers, makers, and cultural practitioners to reflect on the work shaping Jordan's design landscape. The fourth edition, held from October 2 to 17, 2026, marked a new chapter for the event, with architects Sarah Hejazin and Bisher Tabbaa, founders of the architecture and design practice FADAA, serving as co-directors. Their appointment also brought their research-driven approach to the event's broader program, which explored the relationships between daily practices, cultural memories, and material environments. During the event, we had the opportunity to speak with Sarah Hejazin and Bisher Tabbaa about the thinking behind this year's theme, their approach to material investigations, and how practicing in Jordan informs their work across architecture, objects, and public space.

Embracing Playful Imperfection With The CSS `random()` Function

Design systems thrive on consistency, so where does randomness fit in? Through playful demos of organic typography, bouncing letters, and splayed cards, Brecht De Ruyte shows how the new CSS `random()` function brings a little imperfection to the web without JavaScript libraries or preprocessor loops that generate hundreds of lines of static CSS.

title: What I learned teaching AI prototyping at university
text:
What I learned teaching AI prototyping at university

Teaching students how to prototype with AI tools instead of Figma revealed exciting possibilities and uncomfortable trade-offs. It also offered valuable insight into how non-tech people can create apps with generative AI.

I teach digital prototyping to fashion design undergraduates and master’s students at UPM’s Fashion School. My course focuses on exploring app concepts that can enrich the fashion experience. Past project ideas ranged from aesthetic affinity social communities (and dating) and live-action fashion-branded games to smart garment upcycling, VR fashion recommendations, and even a shared laundry app for roommates.

In previous semesters, I asked my students to prototype in Figma and standard design software. This past term, however, we switched to an entirely AI-based toolset, including Google Stitch, Google AI Studio, and Lovable.

The main reason for this change was, as Philip van Allen anticipated in his pre-LLM paper, that new AI design tools (such as Lovable or Bolt) would be much better suited to explore dynamic, interactive behaviors and flows than classic static screen-based design tools like Figma (in its 2025 version). Precious Ogar discusses the approach in more detail in his article AI-Focused Prototyping: A Practical Guide for UI/UX Designers.

The impact of this shift went beyond what I had anticipated and brought a new set of challenges. For starters, generative AI changed the very notion of prototyping: we were no longer building interconnected mockups to simulate an experience, but creating dynamic, functional applications that felt much closer to real products.

More importantly, it also changed how students practiced design skills and thought about product design — potentially for the worse. Greater reliance on tools meant less time spent conceptualizing. Endless prompting and refining replaced the hands-on practice required to master foundational design skills. And those skills are still highly relevant to creating production-quality experiences.

Yet, the final outcome gave my students the genuine confidence that they could build AI-enabled apps themselves — something I find deeply satisfying, and believe to be true.

In the end, the experience convinced me that prototyping with this new generation of tools demands a new kind of design literacy — one that puts more emphasis on thinking about our design than on the mechanics of building it.

Below are some of the key lessons I learned while teaching AI prototyping to fashion design students. They are presented in no particular order and vary in scope and relevance, but I believe each offers valuable insights for educators and designers.

What are we building?

Traditionally, a prototype was just a set of interactive mockups — a quick, low-effort way to test a concept without building an MVP or real app.

But GenAI has blurred that boundary. Today, anybody can create a partially working app in roughly the same time. And because these apps are made up of actual JavaScript and HTML code, they can include real features like live user authentication, persistent storage, and support all types of business logic. In other words, you are creating a conventional web app instead of a classic prototype.

But this impressive capability created a conceptual trap for my students. Many assumed the apps they were creating would inherently possess the same ‘magical’ AI capabilities as the tools used to build them. Some even saw these tools as oracles, as Olmanson et al. observed in their research with design students.

They expected their prototypes to be able to recognize images, perform semantic searches, or generate videos out of the box. They seemingly ignored that GenAI tools generate conventional web apps. Adding true AI functionality required significant setup work that was well beyond our class’s scope

I had to address this misconception directly in the classroom. I needed students to understand what they were building and where its limits were. When their concepts demanded complex AI capabilities, I guided them back to the fundamentals of prototyping: simulate the experience using mockups, predefined states, and pre-generated media.

Even in the age of AI, the golden rule of prototyping still holds: fake it, don’t make it.

The product vision is yours

Inevitably, most students began prototyping with high-level, generic prompts. And they were quickly disappointed by the results. It wasn’t just the visuals or interactions, but the product itself that didn’t match their expectations.

When I asked students to describe the product they wanted to build, it soon became clear that most couldn’t picture it themselves. So I asked them to develop a clearer vision of what they wanted to build. Starting from the home page, write down what information the product would show to the user, and what it would allow them to do. And then, determine the top sections of the app and repeat the same exercise for each.

Once they worked that out, they made much faster progress because they could communicate their intent much more clearly.

The conceptual model is yours too

This leads directly to the next challenge. When it came to specifying detailed app behavior and flows, a recurring challenge was mental model misalignment. Even when students had a clearer idea of how their product should work, AI tools frequently generated something completely different from their intent. Those alternatives could be perfectly reasonable. But they just weren’t right for the product the students were trying to build.

Help came when we discussed how to specify high-level design aspects for their apps. I introduced them to mental models and conceptual models. In a couple of cases, we applied very rudimentary conceptual grammars (mapping out objects, attributes, actions, and relationships). These allowed to map the users' mental models into their apps more effectively and helped the students to prompt more confidently the detailed behaviour they expected from their products.

This lesson also extends to professional designers as well. Generative AI excels at providing average solutions for conventional problems. But if you are designing something complex, novel, or off the beaten path, AI will likely default to standard patterns and miss your intent. To design effectively with AI, having a clear conceptual model is non-negotiable.

Prompting can be intimidating

Because everyone uses apps daily, at first, my students assumed that describing one to an AI tool would be easy. It seemed almost too simple. But after their first few rounds of prompting, that confidence quickly gave way to frustration. The results often fell short of their expectations, and in some cases the outputs were completely different from what they had intended. A similar perception was observed by Olmanson et al. in their research work.

To help, I suggested using LLMs to refine their prompts before feeding them into the prototyping tools. This worked well in some cases. However, a few students ended up endlessly polishing prompts in ChatGPT or Gemini instead of testing them in the actual vibe-coding tool. For some, prompt refinement became a way to avoid confronting the prototype itself.

At that point, I had to remind them that iteration is about improving and evaluating the prototype, the tool’s output, not endlessly perfecting the prompt.

Design vocabulary is essential

One thing that consistently improved the quality of the results was using standard design vocabulary. When students described interfaces in everyday language, the outputs were often mediocre or inconsistent. Once they started using established design terms — such as button group, navigation menu, card, accordion, modal dialog, or splash screen — the AI became much more precise. The same was true for common UI behaviour terms like transition, persistence, overlay, scroll, and animation. And in certain cases, some basic software development vocabulary also proved useful.

This makes a lot of sense since the internal currency of AI tools is language. The more precise our vocabulary, the better they can understand what elements make up an interface and how those elements should behave and respond to user interactions.

Azamnouri et al. (2026) set up a similar AI educational project and also found that their students needed to acquire certain technical capabilities to successfully prototype their app ideas.

English produced better results

Our classes took place in Madrid, and most students naturally wrote their prompts in Spanish. While this was not in any way a controlled study, we noticed that prompts written in English often appeared to produce more accurate results and soon became a practical consideration in class.

This may reflect an implicit bias in AI tools, partly because so much of the material used to train them is in English. And if we see this effect with Spanish, one of the world’s most widely spoken languages, the gap could be even wider for languages with far fewer online resources, such as Catalan or Macedonian. Language support raises a real inclusive design challenge for AI tools.

The value of element targeting

This might seem a minor point, but it offers a very practical lesson. Students often struggled to control the scope of their refinements. The tools would frequently apply modifications well beyond what the students had intended. This reflects how prompting, by its own descriptive nature, doesn’t make it easy to define a precise scope.

Luckily, most modern AI design tools allow you to select a specific on-screen element -a card, button, image, or section- as the target for your prompt.

That small interaction made a big difference. By narrowing the scope before prompting, students got more accurate results and ran into far fewer headaches. It also reinforced an important principle of working with AI: the clearer the context, the better the outcome.

Pricing is an educational problem

Pricing was an important constraint. While preparing the course, I contacted several AI companies, including Lovable, Base44, and Claude, to ask about academic pricing. There were no class-specific plans available, and their standard plans were both expensive and unpredictable for a course where students need to explore freely. Unfortunately, under these conditions, my university denied funding.

This is a serious limitation. Exploration is not an optional part of design education. Students need room to try ideas, make mistakes, discard approaches, and start again. Credit-based pricing in educational settings clearly penalizes that type of experimentation.

Google’s vibe suite

As a result, we ended up using Google’s AI design products extensively, as they offered the most generous and comprehensive free plans. We were going to use Google Stitch anyway. It is Google’s vibe design tool and is particularly valuable for the broad exploration of both visual and interaction concepts, which are essential in the early stages of rapid prototyping. Once a clear direction emerged, students moved on to Google AI Studio, a proper vibe coding tool, to build interactive apps and flesh out their ideas.

On the downside, we did run into some significant performance issues, particularly with Google AI Studio. Our classes took place in the evenings in Madrid (CET), which coincides with morning and central business hours in the US. I can only speculate that we were hitting a period of peak demand for these tools.

Vibe coding is a QA nightmare

Prototyping with AI tools pushed students to adopt a tactic more commonly associated with software development: regression testing.

Modifying a feature in Google AI Studio often alters another part of the app that has already been completed. A new addition could change a layout, break a flow, remove a feature, or modify something that did not seem connected with the prompt. After a few of these incidents, students learned that every important change required a broader review. They had to test the whole app again, not only the feature they had just modified. Also, version bookmarking and history were very helpful in handling some catastrophic updates smoothly.

While code dependencies can partly explain this behaviour, sometimes it seemed quite random. Either way, this is currently the rather frustrating reality of vibe coding that app creators have to deal with.

Is AI prototyping slower?

This was the most shocking outcome of the course. Overall, it took my students slightly longer to create a prototype with AI tools than with Figma.

The reason probably lies in the fact that they were actually building something closer to a complete application rather than an app façade with some interactions, as is typically the case with traditional prototyping.

While vibe coding tools can produce incredible results in the matter of minutes, the process of creating a fully functional prototype clearly involves more decision-making, more debugging, and more testing. It also required students to develop a deeper understanding of the product they were trying to prototype.

AI and designer deskilling

By far, the most concerning lesson was related to the educational experience. Students using AI tools were able to create richer, more complete experiences. They explored more ambitious product concepts and even built working apps. Things that simply weren’t possible using Figma alone.

However, this also meant fewer opportunities to practise core UI design skills like arranging layouts, establishing visual hierarchy by means of size, color, and spacing, or grouping elements by applying the Gestalt principles. In comparison, my previous student cohorts, who used conventional prototyping tools, undoubtedly developed stronger competences in these key areas.

Perhaps, as Lee et al. (2025) evidenced in their work, relying on generative AI tools reduces users' cognitive processes and critical thinking. In the end, this effect may contribute to achieving lower skill levels. Similar concerns were expressed by Slava Polonski in his article “AI skill atrophy: Are we forgetting how to think?”

There is an uncomfortable paradox here. We are currently witnessing how the product designer role is shifting towards a higher level of involvement in the design process, with practitioners potentially being displaced from more tedious UI work. Yet to effectively supervise a design, designers still need a strong grasp of the fundamentals to identify and correct any problems in AI-generated outputs, whether they are conceptual, visual, or related to interaction.

On the other hand, we are facing the possibility of degrading our students’ core design skills. These have traditionally been acquired through hands-on practice with tools such as Figma. The temptation now is to divert curricular time towards AI-based design practice. This creates a real risk of deskilling the very people who will soon be called upon to provide oversight of AI-generated output.

There is a clear implication for design education. We cannot replace core skill learning with AI-based tool practice. But neither can we disregard AI-based design practice because of its enormous potential. Our challenge is to integrate both types of learning into the curriculum to prepare our students for their future role as AI designers.

Final thoughts

Replacing Figma with AI tools turned out to be about more than just speeding up prototyping. It changed the nature of what students were actually building. Instead of creating only the façade of an experience, they were able to build functional applications that could look surprisingly close to real products. A key takeaway was that students need to understand what AI tools are actually creating, how and when to incorporate AI-related features, and when a convincing simulation is a better choice.

The students who made the most progress were the ones who developed a clear product vision and some form of a conceptual model. Being able to explain what their product should show and how it should behave turned them into more effective builders. Design vocabulary, prompting in English, targeting specific elements, and limited refinement of prompts in LLMs proved useful in most cases.

At the same time, this experience also revealed a less attractive side to vibe coding. Building a functional prototype requires more decisions, testing, and debugging than creating a conventional interactive mockup. That often means more effort and time. Credit-based pricing and unreliable performance also limited the exploratory work that our course relies on. And because AI tools handle much of the detailed UI work, students spent less time practising the visual and interaction-design fundamentals they may need in the future.

This is the core takeaway for design educators. We need to preserve the hands-on practice through which students develop design fundamentals, while teaching them how to use AI tools responsibly and effectively. We cannot treat these as competing approaches: students need both.

Despite all these drawbacks, I found the final outcome genuinely encouraging. My students left the course feeling capable of turning a product idea into an MVP app by themselves. I believe that confidence, colored by the understanding of the possibilities and limitations of these tools, was the most valuable thing they gained.

Resources

  • Azamnouri, A., Hörauf, D., Schönberger, B., Bogner, J., & Wagner, S. (2026). Teaching AI competencies: Experiences from coaching interdisciplinary teams to develop AI prototypes.
  • Lee, H.-P., Sarkar, A., Tankelevitch, L., Drosos, I., Rintel, S., Banks, R., & Wilson, N. (2025). The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking: Self-Reported Reductions in Cognitive Effort and Confidence Effects From a Survey of Knowledge Workers.
  • Nielsen Norman Group (2025). AI Prototyping in Real Design Contexts.
  • Olmanson, J., Hassani, A., & Larsen, G. (2025). Learning educational technology prototyping with generative AI.
  • Ogar, P. (2025). AI-Focused Prototyping: A Practical Guide for UI/UX Designers.
  • Polonski, Slava (2026). AI skill atrophy: Are we forgetting how to think?
  • Van Allen, P. (2018). Ways of prototyping AI. Interactions.

title: State of a system
text:
State of a system

Almost eight years ago, I started working on a design system that I got the opportunity to revisit just a few years later. The second round became as big a push with far fewer people. Now, three years after ending the work I’m finally ready to share that experience.

My thesis:

  • A rigid design kit is a cache of design decisions, prone to becoming obsolete with the requirements constantly evolving.
  • Documenting practices and boundaries leaves powerless responsibility for upholding coherence to designers and developers.
  • Governing an LLM skill could be a better basis for an evolving design system than components, code or documentation alone.

Back when I wrote my first Medium article about design systems, I was in the middle of a year spent extending a design system towards more consumer-driven businesses. Since then, I have wandered off to design other types of products and services, some design languages too. I changed employers twice before I got handed the chance to return to work on the next version of the very same design system I had stopped working on a few years prior. That work extended for another 12–18 months, after which it has continued its life without me knowing much about it. Almost ever since, I’ve had this article as an early draft that I’m now ready to fill in. Only now, with the latest technological advances, do I think I have found a way around the biggest challenge with the work delivered: it simply grew massive by having too many variants to answer the backing requirements.

Where my first leg was about expanding the design language to new market segments, the task for the second leg was to consolidate various design kits into a single kit. First expanding, then converging. This is nothing new for a design consultant such yours truly.

The concepts from my previous work for this client had helped the design core group to form a “Style evolution” booklet guiding future projects, after which the core group dissolved as the company restructured itself. Since then the business units had taken it forward to form their own design kits, some ending up being more advanced than others. In practice the design had divided into multiple design kits, with each business unit aiming for the future cloud-based software on its own. Each design kit relied on the same core tokens and design drivers from earlier. What differed from earlier was a design council with representatives from each business unit responsible for design decisions, instead of a single centralised group.

Personally it was delightful to see that the concepts from the first leg had lived on. But unlike earlier, it seemed that the goal of having a single code-based truth had been abandoned in favour of aligning the work through design phases. This felt odd, since their move to browser-based cloud applications would favour a shared codebase compared to the embedded nature of software from earlier, built on three code frameworks: WPF, Angular and React. Given the magnitude and scale, simply focusing on the design aspect might have seemed the more accessible path to take. But in retrospect, the intricate variations and complexity would have been managed much more easily in code. Especially now, when an LLM helps draft many of these.

The time was not ready for any of this when we started the consolidation work in 2022. Our task was to consolidate the individual kits manually into a single company-wide design kit. During less than a year of crafting, with help from a few colleagues at DK&A, we ended up designing and documenting around 40 components, applicable to theming and mode switching through native Figma library swaps. There was a structure of core components distributed to each design kit file, making the whole system a bit more manageable, but also prone to break. With everything wired, the overall structure delivered was comprehensive but demanding to govern. We even delivered skeleton models of the components to be handled similarly with a library swap. The end result was a sound number of components with a massive number of variations and properties, such as Focus, baked into each of them. Not hundreds of variants, but nearly two thousand in total.

Variations themselves had been a staple of the system from the get-go. To handle the multiple different size variants in Figma you still had to have multiple assets to apply these values feasibly. This was the main cause of massiveness with the kit, which in coded components could be overcome with a simple set of token variables. When we started the project, Figma already had boolean component properties to simply turn items on and off within the components. At its heaviest the working file held around 4,000 variants, with the delivered design kit holding 1,786 variants. A reduction of just over half. With typography variables launched in April 2024, less than a year after our project ended, most of the size variants could have been handled similarly to tokens. The 1,786 variants could have been cut to as little as a fifth by just handling the size and typography variations with variables alone.

The most absurd example of all the delivered components was the button. In total 260 variants of it. Three behaviours: default, split and toggle all divided into 5 different sizes with a varying number of properties in them. Only 15 of those needed real thinking: text sizes, spacing, proportions. The other 245 were arithmetic. Arithmetic can express a decision. It cannot make one.

Not all of the roughly 40 components were similarly burdened with variants. Some could be mostly handled by boolean component properties, others being complex for the sake of flexing Figma to its limits. We even experimented with a card component, which in the end was deemed too impractical for scaling due to the sub-component structure. Looking back, it would have been much easier to describe the desired function as a prompt, but it would surely have left some memorable moments in problem solving unexperienced.

Nonetheless, since then I’ve heavily streamlined the design kits I’ve worked with. Thinking from a lean, progressive perspective rather than aiming to bake all the requirements in. Nowadays the components can be very crude, but in their simplicity capable of taking in many variations without sacrificing the base functionality. Figma has since launched slots: virtually fully editable frames inside a component that users are free to play around with without meddling with the core component. Even the card component, which was deemed too impractical earlier, became feasible just a few years later.

During the project Figma slots were only dreamed of and sub-components were the standard way forward. This was a technical limitation more than a design decision. Had it been possible to approach the task with a more lightweight structure and fewer variables, I would have leaned even then towards such a structure. This would have asked more of the documentation setting boundaries for edits, and of the stakeholders managing them. Having an LLM in the mix, you could have baked the limits into a skill, but would testing the limits have been a less demanding task than crafting the needed variants? Maybe, but needs confirmation.

Replacing the native Figma library swap with Figma’s native variables for theming would have made the total number of system files a lot lighter. We know this because Figma released variable theming midway through the process. We tested it, but could not pivot the system to use it. It was too late to turn the ship around and start refactoring everything. In a third iteration, variable theming would be an obvious choice. Though the skeleton components would then need to be applied differently. I’m questioning whether they were required to be supported in Figma at all.

For a design council, a true cross-organisation ownership requires a lot from the individual stakeholders and their communication skills. An almost altruistic mindset towards decision making is needed to overcome otherwise natural group dynamics. Another key for a global design council to function is to have a shared culture taking into account the diversity of team members in different time zones, cultural environments or calendar routines. Democratic decision-making needs time, so a slower pace should not be made an issue. Too fast movements and non-holistic design choices become a mess over time. Group governing design is always a delicate process as designers tend to fall in love with their creations. Me being not much different.

We were the hired hands doing the actual consolidation work, so much of the decision-making was in the end in our hands. You need to be hands-deep in solving the challenges to be able to call the shots. And to do a lot of lobbying to get stakeholders invested in design decisions. Still, it was consolidation work and a single design kit could only bend in so many ways back in 2023.

Though the consolidation task was a challenge, by no means do I regret doing it. It has shaped my approach for similar tasks ever since, something I touched in on my previous article. With what is possible nowadays, I’m able to put what I learned into action in my design process.

A lot has been written in hindsight already, but I want to conclude this writing with a “what if”. Technically I have already brought up several Figma-specific updates that would allow building things differently nowadays. But it has to be questioned: does anybody use Figma anymore? Reading almost any designer’s LinkedIn would incline so. I have long been inclined to think that a true design system only lives in code format. Anything else is just middleware. But nowadays, when code and design can be produced on the fly, is code just an output format among others? Compared with Figma assets, it is still a step closer to the end users. But is it the single source of truth anymore? If an LLM could be used to produce components and layouts as well as design assets for any given design software through MCP, should it be considered the single source of truth instead? Another project to rebuild an existing system for the LLM age would be needed to prove any of this. If not for the very same design system, then any other of similar size. You can call me up.

Next, I will revisit my first Medium article and write about how design systems could become the best enablers instead of limiting designers’ freedom in problem solving. Thanks to my ex-colleague Konrad Wysokinski for fact-checking this article and to Claude for the proofreading and sparring.

title: Virtue ethics in everyday interface design
text:
Virtue ethics in everyday interface design

How wording, hierarchy, and moments of friction can support considered action.

One thing that troubles me about designers is how readily some treat public expressions of moral conviction as evidence of sound ethical judgment. They announce their commitments to causes they regard as worthy, speak confidently about responsible practice, yet fail to examine their own biases or the ethical tensions within their decisions.

Virtue signaling is not a substitute for reflective ethical judgment.

Claiming the moral high ground does not demonstrate the judgment needed to question one’s assumptions, recognize competing values, or explain why particular priorities should guide someone else’s experience.

As designers, our convictions carry weight because we make decisions for other people. We determine what an interface makes visible, which actions it encourages, where it asks someone to reflect, and what it handles automatically.

These choices can support one value while limiting another, such as protecting someone from harm while restricting their autonomy. People encounter these decisions whether or not they or the wider society share the designer’s values, and good intentions alone cannot tell us whether we have exercised that authority well.

Examining that authority requires asking what our work ultimately serves. Human flourishing, understood broadly as living well, offers a shared aspiration toward which design can contribute, even when we disagree about what living well involves. That aspiration extends beyond satisfaction with an experience or success at an isolated task.

Both creating an experience and engaging with it offer opportunities to exercise ethical judgment. Beyond addressing user needs, we might ask what these activities allow designers and the people who encounter their work to exercise, learn, or become.

Virtue ethics provides a way to approach this question because it connects human flourishing with the development of character and practical wisdom. Virtues are qualities such as honesty, justice, and courage, while practical wisdom, or phronesis, involves discerning what constitutes good action in particular circumstances.

In the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle explains that moral virtues develop through repeated action. We become disposed to act justly by acting justly, though he also emphasizes that acting virtuously requires knowledge and choice, not merely reproducing outward behavior.

Thomas Aquinas develops the Aristotelian tradition within a theological account of human life, distinguishing virtues acquired through human action from virtues received through divine grace. His account of acquired virtue helps clarify how repeated actions can cultivate dispositions that shape how we approach later situations. This shifts attention from an isolated interaction to the habits participation may help sustain.

For designers, this raises two connected responsibilities. The first concerns how we exercise virtue in our own work—through careful deliberation, consideration for others, and acceptance of responsibility for the consequences of our decisions. The second concerns the opportunities our designs provide for others to do the same.

A designer may act conscientiously while producing an experience that gives users little room to deliberate or develop judgment. We therefore need to consider both the ethical quality of our own practice and how the resulting experience supports the ethical development of those who use it.

Before considering how design might support these qualities, it is reasonable to ask why we should regard them as good in the first place. In Dependent Rational Animals, Alasdair MacIntyre argues that our vulnerability, dependence on others, and capacity to reason help explain why we need virtues. We rely on relationships through which we receive care, learn, and develop judgment.

Honesty, justice, and generosity help sustain those relationships and the human goods they make possible. Their value, in this sense, rests on what human beings need to live and develop well. This offers reasons for valuing these qualities without settling every disagreement about what living well means.

For designers, the connection lies in how people participate in those relationships and activities through the interfaces we create. Communicating, learning, and working together involve opportunities to exercise judgment, honesty, and care for others. Interfaces cannot make someone virtuous, but their wording, available actions, and visual hierarchy can make these considerations more prominent or easier to overlook.

Consider a hypothetical social platform where someone has clicked Share on an article. Figure 1 compares two possible sharing dialogs.

In Option A, a dialog headed “Share this article?” displays the article’s source and headline, followed by a solid blue “Share now” button and a “Cancel” action. The interface asks the person to confirm whether they want to share, without drawing attention to whether they have read the article.

Option B retains the same heading and article preview but adds a message: “You haven’t opened this article. Would you like to read it before sharing?” A solid blue “Read article” button appears above an outlined “Share now” button, with “Cancel” beneath both. This version changes the wording, adds an action, and gives reading the strongest visual emphasis. The person can still share immediately, but the interface explicitly invites them to consider reading the article before passing it along.

As designers, we are often trained to reduce friction and help people accomplish their goals efficiently. If someone wants to share an article, the familiar response is to make sharing as straightforward as possible. Yet sharing information also affects the people who encounter it, which gives designers a responsibility to consider what the interface encourages along the way. The immediate task is to circulate an article, but completing it efficiently does not determine whether the experience supports responsible participation.

The concern extends beyond whether a particular article contains misinformation. An interface that consistently encourages circulation without examination may also encourage a passive relationship to knowledge, in which people pass along claims without considering their meaning, evidence, or credibility.

A virtue ethics perspective asks what habits such interactions invite people to develop. Does the experience give someone an occasion to exercise intellectual honesty and care for others, or does it make those considerations easy to overlook in the pursuit of immediate action?

Seeking to support these qualities also carries a danger. Designers may take this as permission to decide how others ought to behave, imposing a narrow account of proper behavior, particularly when users have little ability to question or refuse it.

Designers therefore need humility about the limits of their knowledge and power, together with a willingness to explain and examine the goods their decisions serve. Supporting ethical agency requires attention to the user’s capacity to understand, deliberate, and act, including circumstances in which the user reaches a different conclusion from the designer.

Human flourishing gives this discussion a broader purpose, but invoking it does not settle what a particular design should do. Practical wisdom requires contextual judgment that considers the people, circumstances, and competing goods involved — a general principle alone cannot determine the appropriate response.

We still have to explain which human capacities an experience supports, why those capacities matter, and how the design contributes to their exercise. Character develops through relationships and circumstances far beyond any individual product, and users do not need a moral lesson in every interaction.

Designers shape some of the conditions under which people learn, communicate, work, and make decisions. That responsibility calls for ethical judgment in our own work and attention to the opportunities our designs give others to exercise judgment themselves. Alongside asking whether someone can complete a task easily, we should ask what their participation allows them to practice, and whether that practice contributes to living well.

We must also continually examine what we understand as good, articulate why we believe it is good, and remain open to questioning those beliefs. Our understanding of how design contributes to living well is part of an ongoing conversation, and participating in that conversation is part of our responsibility.

title: How to design transparent AI cost controls
text:
How to design transparent AI cost controls

A practical guide to choosing usage units, designing spending limits, and explaining AI costs before, during, and after the work.

Every AI response has a price. People often discover it only when a limit hits or a bill arrives.

A quick edit and a long-running agent can look almost identical in the interface. One finishes in seconds. The other might read hundreds of files, call external tools, and retry steps along the way. Yet both start with the same button.

Meanwhile, AI products keep changing what they charge for: requests, credits, tasks, usage allowances. Showing more technical numbers won’t make those costs easier to understand. People want to know what a job might use, whether it’s worth running, and what they can do to spend less.

For designers, that comes down to two decisions:

  1. The unit: what users see themselves spending.
  2. The moment: when they understand the cost — before, during, or after the work.

Under the hood: what a token is

A token is a unit a model reads or generates. A tokenizer breaks text into pieces: words, parts of words, punctuation, sometimes even spaces. For English, a useful rough estimate is that one token represents about three-quarters of a word. So a million text tokens might represent around 750,000 English words. The exact count depends on the tokenizer, language, and content.

  • Input and output cost different amounts. Model providers commonly charge more for tokens they generate than tokens they read. On several current models, output is about five times the price of standard input. Longer answers, reasoning, and repeated attempts can change the economics of what looks like one request.
  • Model choice matters. Output-token prices can differ by tens of times — or more — across models. A request that is cheap in a lightweight model can cost considerably more in a frontier model. The user’s task hasn’t changed, but the meter has.
  • Modality changes the calculation. Text, images, audio, and video don’t share one universal token conversion. A short prompt, an image attachment, and a five-minute clip may all look like inputs to the same composer, yet require very different amounts of processing. Some providers charge by tokens, others by frames, seconds, or generation settings.

For a sense of scale, a 15-word prompt might be around 20 text tokens. A 1092 × 1092 image has been estimated at roughly 1,600 image tokens using one image-accounting method. For video, Google’s published static-processing examples imply roughly 30,000–90,000 tokens for five minutes, depending on the resolution setting. Those estimates come from different systems, so they cannot be priced as though they were the same kind of token. That limitation is part of the lesson: a single input box hides very different work.

Why showing tokens fails

Tokens are the system’s currency, not the user’s. People budget in money, time, attention, and finished work. They feel the effects of tokens through longer waits, changing quotas, and unexpected charges — not by counting them.

“382,000 tokens used” may be technically precise. It doesn’t tell someone whether the next research run will fit within their allowance, which part of the job was expensive, or what to change next time.

The job isn’t just to disclose a number. It’s to translate system cost into something people can make decisions with.

Predictability beats precision

There’s a useful parallel outside AI. In a study of 10,882 internet subscribers, Lambrecht and Skiera (2006) found that many customers chose a flat-rate plan even when a metered plan would have been cheaper. In one group, nearly half made that choice; more than half of them paid at least twice what they needed to.

The researchers described two reasons:

  • Insurance effect: paying more can feel worthwhile if it removes the risk of a variable bill.
  • Taxi meter effect: people enjoy a service less when they have to watch the meter climb.

The study was about internet tariffs, not AI, so it doesn’t prove how AI subscribers behave. But it captures a tension designers know well: people want to understand what they’re spending without being forced to calculate every interaction.

A good AI cost interface gives them that predictability without pretending the underlying costs are fixed.

Decision 1: choose the unit

Before designing a meter or a pricing screen, decide what people see themselves spending.

There isn’t one perfect unit. Raw tokens expose the model’s actual consumption, which is useful in API consoles but hard to reason about in a product workflow. Dollars are easier to recognize, especially for teams managing a budget, but the amount can still change from one run to the next.

Some products charge in natural units such as minutes of audio, pages processed, or GPU time. Others use credits: a product-specific currency that lets very different AI features draw from one balance. Credits simplify billing, but people have to learn what they’re worth.

Closer to the work itself are tasks and actions — one generation, enrichment, or run — and outcomes, where a charge depends on a defined result. These are easier to count because they resemble what the user asked for. They also shift more uncertainty to the vendor: a 200-page document and a one-page email might both count as one summary, despite costing very different amounts to process.

At the other end are usage allowances, where people work within a pool or reset window, and invisible usage, where a feature is included without showing a meter at all.

The important distinction is who carries the uncertainty. Tokens and metered dollars pass more of it to the user. Tasks and outcomes put more of it on the vendor. A usage allowance protects people from per-action calculations, but can leave them guessing when they’ll hit the limit.

Neither end works for everything. That’s why many products use a hybrid approach — an included allowance for everyday work, with separate limits or paid usage for expensive actions.

When to show a price — and when to hide it

A visible cost makes people more careful. That’s helpful for an expensive batch, but exhausting for everyday chat.

For discrete, potentially expensive work — enriching 500 rows, rendering a video, or scheduling a nightly automation — show the price or a credible range before the user commits. That number matters to the decision.

For frequent, exploratory actions like chatting, small edits, or code suggestions, a usage allowance is often better. Putting a price on every interaction turns experimentation into budgeting. But when one job is unusually expensive, even inside a subscription, make an exception: show its likely cost before it starts. The goal isn’t to hide spending; it’s to show it when someone can still act on it.

Usage limits

Instead of pricing each action, the product gives users a pool and shows how much remains. It’s familiar from subscriptions and easy to understand — until the pool disappears unexpectedly.

Where it fits: Consumer and prosumer plans with frequent, exploratory actions.
What good looks like: Users can tell what’s left, when it resets, and what will happen at the limit.
Why it works. Limits remove the need to do arithmetic every time someone sends a message. The user can focus on the work, with a fairly predictable subscription price.

  • Show each time window and its reset. Claude uses short session limits alongside weekly limits. A line such as “resets in 1 hr 36 min” beside “resets Friday at 8:00 AM” gives people a plan. “Resets soon” doesn’t.
  • Separate genuinely different pools. In the examples above, Cursor distinguishes model usage categories and Claude breaks out a top-model allowance. That helps users connect a decision — using a more expensive model — to the quota it affects. Don’t split pools simply because the billing system happens to have multiple internal counters.
  • Explain the overflow order. Show what is consumed first, what happens next, whether on-demand spending is enabled, and where an actual cap applies. Users shouldn’t need to infer the order from three settings screens.
  • Give temporary promotions an end date. Claude advertises a temporary higher allowance. Stating when standard limits return avoids making the end of a promotion feel like a stealth reduction.
  • Offer an alternative to upgrading. A saved or banked reset in Codex can restore eligible usage windows, subject to plan and expiry rules. Waiting for the reset, switching modes, or reducing scope can be just as important

Tasks and outcomes

Per-action units count something users already recognize: a generation, enrichment, run, or task. The appeal is that the decision and the charge use the same language.

Where it fits: Automations and actions that are easy to count.
What good looks like: Someone can estimate a month’s workload and get close to the bill.

Zapier is a useful reference. In the captured plan, the interface shows “Included tasks: 119 / 750” and “Additional tasks ($0.05/task): 0 / 1,500.” Users can distinguish the included pool from overflow, see the unit price, and understand the potential ceiling.

The more important detail is what Zapier doesn’t count. Triggers, filters, and certain built-in steps don’t count as tasks; successful action steps generally do, while errored steps don’t. Those rules answer a question that matters as much as the price: who pays for failure?

Why it works. An action is legible. If the same action consistently costs the same amount, users can forecast and compare.

Do: Explain what counts, what doesn’t, and how failed or repeated attempts are treated. Give overages their own unit price and ceiling.

Don’t: Call something an outcome if customers can’t independently tell whether it happened.

Credits

Credits let a product use one balance across different features: chat, app building, hosting, deployments, enrichment, or external services. They’re useful, but no one arrives with an intuition for what one credit is worth.

Where it fits: Products offering several expensive AI features under one account.
What good looks like: Users understand both the credit’s approximate value and why a particular action consumed it.

Why it works. Credits make unlike actions comparable and let providers adjust underlying costs without rebuilding the subscription. The left-hand screenshot shows several pools — daily, monthly, rollover, and top-ups — with different expiry rules. The right-hand example attributes deductions to projects and jobs and maintains a running balance. That’s useful accounting.

Where it breaks. The screenshots show several familiar problems:

  • No transferable sense of value. A 50-credit pack priced at $30 works out to $0.60 per credit. A different product’s 3,000-credit pack for $500 is about $0.17 per credit. The name is the same, but the unit isn’t. These are snapshot prices from the illustrations, not a shared market rate.
  • Fractional deductions without context. “Agent Call: −0.77” is precise but doesn’t tell users what the call achieved.
  • Unexplained differences. A deployment costs 50 credits and an agent call costs 0.77. A ledger can record that difference without helping anyone understand it.
  • Promotions mixed into accounting. A “20% More” top-up offer belongs in the purchasing flow. On a usage-history screen, it competes with the reason someone opened that screen: checking where the balance went.

Decision 2: choose the moment

Choosing a unit answers what users spend. Next comes when they learn about it.

There are three chances to communicate cost: before, during, and after the work. Ignore them and the user finds out at a fourth moment: the wall, when the allowance runs out or an unexpected charge appears.

Before the work, help people judge the likely cost while they can still change the scope. Explain what drives it, use a range when the total is uncertain, and offer a cheaper mode, a smaller run, or a spending ceiling.

During the work, show meaningful progress instead of an unreliable countdown. Let long jobs run without keeping people on the same screen. Make it clear what stopping will cost, and ask before continuing if the original estimate no longer holds.

After the work, show what was delivered and what it cost. Explain unusual charges, make reused work or savings visible, say how failures are billed, and keep a history people can return to. These are the three moments the illustration brings together.

Before: model selectors, effort controls, and previews

Before a run begins, the user can still change the scope. Three controls are especially useful.

Model selectors. A dropdown of model names can force people into an engineering decision. Not everyone wants that. In August 2025, OpenAI launched GPT-5 with automatic routing, then quickly brought back clearer choices such as Auto, Fast, and Thinking alongside more detailed model controls. The lesson isn’t that model choice should disappear. It’s that most users benefit from an outcome-oriented default, while advanced users still need access to the underlying models.

Effort controls. Effort dials are becoming increasingly common in AI products, but what they actually control remains a mystery to many users. Cursor offers a scale from Low to Extra High, other interfaces use sliders, while deep-research modes make the choice more implicit. All give users some control over how much time and computation a model spends on a task. But what does High really mean compared to Medium? Will the result be noticeably better, take longer, or simply consume more of the user’s allowance? The controls are becoming more familiar, but the trade-offs behind them are still poorly explained.

Previews before large spend. Deep-research screen gives users a plan they can edit before an agent starts reading sources. That’s a strong moment to intervene. The two missing pieces are cost and consent. A plan with five steps doesn’t reveal whether cutting one will save much. And for a genuinely costly job, an auto-start countdown can turn doing nothing into agreement.

A good preflight makes the trade-off concrete: what’s included, what’s optional, what the approximate total could be, and what will happen if the job needs more.

Clay is a useful reference for pricing before execution. In the captured interface, enrichments show figures such as “0.5 / row,” “~3 / row,” or “varies by model.” A recurring signal displays its monthly cost before activation. These labels tell the truth about uncertainty rather than presenting every action as fixed-price.

The same principle applies to scheduled work. Show the likely monthly spend of an hourly or nightly automation, not just its price per execution. Small recurring charges are easy to overlook.

During: progress, cancellations, and changing forecasts

This is the thinnest part of many AI cost experiences. A run starts, a spinner appears, and all the useful controls return only when it’s finished.

Show real units of progress when they exist: 320 of 500 contacts processed, 12 sources checked, three files edited. For open-ended work, show meaningful phases instead of a percentage you’ve invented. Let long jobs move out of the foreground without losing their status.

Where costs accrue as the job runs, display usage so far and the remaining budget or cap. A forecast can change if an agent discovers extra work. When the expected cost moves well beyond the original range — or reaches an agreed checkpoint — pause and ask whether to continue. Don’t silently treat the original approval as unlimited permission.

After: receipts

The receipt connects a charge to the work it paid for. It’s also what helps people make a better choice next time.

  • Per action, right next to the result. Replit’s captured run summary lists “13 actions” and what changed; a message menu shows “Worked for 43s” and “Credits used 0.50.” The receipt is available where the work happened.
  • Per session, with cost drivers. Another captured panel shows 3,450 credits alongside context used by instructions, tools, messages, files, and tool results. The surprising insight isn’t the total; it’s what consumed the context. A Compact Conversation control gives the user a way to respond.
  • Per period, with searchable history. Clay’s usage history can be examined by time, column, run, or provider and exported. That’s what a team lead needs when someone asks why the workspace budget changed.

A breakdown with a way to act is a receipt. A breakdown without one is a report.

For most users, keep the first layer light. Put the deduction and result together; make the technical breakdown one click away; put exportable history where teams already manage billing.

Do: Attach a light receipt to the result, reveal cost drivers on demand, and record the failure policy.

Put it to work

As AI products move toward longer, more autonomous workflows, the cost of a single action becomes harder to predict. What looks like one request can involve dozens of steps, multiple models, and external tools. Traditional usage meters weren’t designed to explain that complexity.

The challenge isn’t simply to expose more information. It’s to help people understand what they’re spending, why costs vary, and which choices are within their control.

Across the examples we’ve explored, one principle stands out: cost should be visible when it matters, without becoming something users have to think about constantly.

Good cost transparency isn’t about making every charge predictable. It’s about making uncertainty understandable, so people can make informed decisions without needing to understand the system underneath.
